T HE escape of an awaiting-trial inmate during proceedings at a court in Edo State is another damning indictment of Nigeria’s dysfunctional criminal justice system. Even more disturbing is the failure of the Nigerian Correctional Service to recapture the fugitive after the embarrassing incident. This is not merely a professional lapse; it is a serious security breach that undermines public confidence in the administration of justice and exposes the country to avoidable danger. A statement by the spokesman of the NCoS Edo State Command, Aminu Suleman, dated October 21, disclosed that Thomas Osita, 28, an awaiting-trial inmate at the Medium Security Custodial Centre, Auchi, escaped “during his appearance in court for trial for the offence of conspiracy and stealing.” Every day Osita remains at large further diminishes the credibility of the correctional authorities and raises troubling questions about their capacity to secure persons in lawful custody. Suspects on the run are a potential menace to society, particularly when they have reason to fear prosecution. One of the 1,993 inmates released by #EndSARS protesters in 2020 subsequently killed a witness who testified against him in court. That tragic precedent should not be lost on the authorities. The Edo State Command must therefore intensify efforts to apprehend Osita and establish how he escaped in broad daylight, apparently under the watch of security operatives. It must also review security arrangements for the movement and production of inmates in court. The incident is particularly alarming against the background of repeated jailbreaks and inmate escapes across the country. The circumstances surrounding the escape are yet to be satisfactorily explained. The News Agency of Nigeria quoted an unnamed correctional official as saying that the officer on duty could not abandon other inmates to pursue Osita without exposing them to danger. The official also blamed inadequate manpower, calling for urgent intervention to prevent a recurrence. The manpower shortage is real. Worse, more than 1,000 correctional personnel are reportedly due for retirement by the end of the year. But staffing constraints cannot serve as a blanket excuse for a security failure of this magnitude. If the authorities cannot safely convey an inmate to court, supervise proceedings and return him to custody, the integrity of the entire correctional process is in question. The safety of inmates, court officials and members of the public is not negotiable. Make PUNCH part of your everyday experience. Anything less would amount to another bureaucratic exercise in damage control. The public deserves answers, not excuses. In the United States and other developed jurisdictions, suspects are routinely restrained with handcuffs, waist chains or leg irons during transportation from detention facilities to court, subject to applicable laws and risk assessments. Such precautions are intended to prevent escape and protect the public. However, restraints inside the courtroom are governed by a different principle: the presumption of innocence and the dignity of the accused. Section 34(1)(a) of the 1999 Constitution guarantees the right to dignity of the human person and prohibits torture or inhuman and degrading treatment. Similarly, Section 5 of the Administration of Criminal Justice Act 2015 provides that a suspect or defendant shall not be handcuffed, bound or otherwise restrained except where there is reasonable apprehension of violence or an attempt to escape, or by order of the court. These safeguards are necessary in a democracy. An accused person is not a convicted criminal, and the state cannot dispense with fundamental rights merely because someone is facing prosecution. But the law equally places a responsibility on correctional authorities to assess risks and provide adequate security. The presumption of innocence does not mean the presumption of an absence of risk. Indeed, Osita’s escape has exposed the consequences of inadequate risk assessment and poor security coordination. Once recaptured, the authorities and the court must properly assess the circumstances before deciding whether any of the statutory exceptions to the prohibition on restraints apply. The incident should not become a pretext for indiscriminately shackling every defendant. Unfortunately, the application of these provisions in Nigeria is often arbitrary and selective. Some suspects are chained hand and foot while being taken to court, while others appear without restraints despite the seriousness of the allegations against them. In some instances, politically exposed persons are conspicuously shackled by anti-corruption agencies, while other suspects are treated with considerably less security. This inconsistency raises questions about whether security decisions are based on objective risk assessments or the status and public profile of the accused. More fundamentally, the Osita incident has exposed a disturbing weakness in security arrangements around Nigerian courtrooms. Correctional officers are not the only security personnel attached to the courts. The police and other relevant agencies also have responsibilities. Where were they when the inmate escaped? Was there any coordinated security plan for the proceedings, or was the correctional officer effectively left to manage the situation alone? Tinubu’s N50,000 relief for the vulnerable Two inmates escape from Kogi custodial centre NDLEA arrests 75 suspected drug traffickers in Edo A courtroom should never become an escape route for suspects, much less a place where security can be so easily breached. The possibility of an accused person escaping is bad enough; the prospect of a suspect entering a courtroom with a weapon or using the proceedings to attack a witness, judge or other court official is even more frightening. Security agencies must not wait for such a tragedy before taking preventive measures. The police should declare Osita wanted and deploy the necessary intelligence and operational resources to track him down. Three weeks without a breakthrough is unacceptable. The fugitive must not be allowed to disappear into the system, while the authorities engage in mutual blame. The problem, however, goes beyond this particular escape. Nigeria’s correctional facilities and justice infrastructure have suffered decades of neglect, overcrowding, inadequate staffing and poor funding. According to the BBC, thousands of inmates have escaped from Nigerian custodial facilities since 2020. Among the major incidents were the escape of 108 inmates from Suleja Custodial Centre in April 2024 following heavy rainfall and structural damage, and the release of hundreds of prisoners in an attack on a correctional facility in Abuja in 2022. Premium Times has also reported that only 984 of the 4,369 inmates who escaped from various custodial facilities between January 2020 and December 2022 were recaptured. If these figures are accurate, they point to a deeply troubling failure of the correctional system to account for persons entrusted to its custody. The scale of the problem is further illustrated by the 2021 attacks on correctional facilities. On April 5, gunmen attacked the Owerri Custodial Centre with explosives and dynamite, freeing 1,884 inmates. On September 12, attackers stormed the Medium Security Custodial Centre in Kabba, Kogi State, released 240 inmates and killed two prison officials. On October 22, another attack on the Abolongo Custodial Centre in Oyo State resulted in the escape of 837 inmates. These incidents exposed the vulnerability of facilities that should be among the most secure public institutions in the country. The condition of the infrastructure is equally disturbing. A 2024 statement by the Suleja custodial authorities acknowledged that several facilities were built during the colonial era and had deteriorated badly. The National Bureau of Statistics has also documented overcrowding in correctional facilities, particularly in southern Nigeria. Custodial centres are not the only places where the safety and dignity of suspects are compromised. On September 16 and 17, 37 suspected illegal miners reportedly suffocated to death at a Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps facility in Minna, Niger State. Such deaths highlight the dangerous consequences of inadequate detention conditions, poor ventilation and institutional indifference. There is also a disturbing history of escapes and attempted escapes from court premises. On December 6, 2017, a 41-year-old suspect, Wasiu Alowonle, accused of stealing iron rods worth N40,000, jumped from a court building at the Ogba Magistrate’s Court in Lagos and died. In January 2024, Oluwatobi Ayoko, 25, reportedly attempted to jump from the top floor of the Lagos High Court. These incidents underscore the need to review not only the security of custodial facilities but also the physical safety and operational arrangements of court premises. Nigeria cannot continue to run a criminal justice system in which suspects escape from courtrooms, prisons are breached with alarming ease, detention facilities become death traps, and thousands of fugitives remain unaccounted for. Such failures embolden criminals, endanger witnesses and law-abiding citizens, and erode confidence in the capacity of the state to enforce its laws. The Federal Government must urgently address the chronic shortage of correctional personnel, rehabilitate dilapidated facilities, improve surveillance and intelligence gathering, and establish clear, coordinated security protocols for court appearances. The police, correctional service and court authorities must work as a coordinated security network rather than isolated institutions passing responsibility after every breach. Ultimately, the escape of Osita must not be dismissed as another unfortunate incident or buried under the familiar excuse of inadequate manpower. It is a warning that Nigeria’s criminal justice system is failing at keeping those lawfully in custody secure while ensuring that justice is served. Until accountability replaces excuses and institutional reform replaces crisis management, the courtroom and the custodial centre will remain vulnerable links in a justice system already struggling to command public confidence. Punch Editorial Board
